episode_title: Ebola in Leiden, a Box 3 Climbdown, and the Bolle Jos Aid Freeze
description: An aid worker with Ebola is being treated in strict isolation in Leiden, and Finance Minister Heinen backs down on taxing small savers. The EU has stopped payments to Sierra Leone, and nobody agrees on why. We also cover Eli Lilly's pill factory in Katwijk, a new test for freelancers, record-low rivers, what young Amsterdammers are taking, a surgical first from Nijmegen, the Batavia's final voyage and what's on in Amsterdam tonight.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: An aid worker with Ebola is in strict isolation in Leiden. The finance minister backs down on taxing small savers. And Brussels has stopped paying Sierra Leone, though nobody agrees why.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And somewhere in the middle of it all, a fugitive drug lord called Bolle Jos.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Friday, the second of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start with Ebola, and a patient who's now being treated in Leiden.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ebola, here? Who is it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: An aid worker for Doctors Without Borders, or MSF, who was infected in the Democratic Republic of Congo. They were flown in on a French private plane, about nine and a half hours in the air, and landed at Schiphol around a quarter to eight on Thursday evening. Then the Marechaussee, the military police who also patrol the airport, escorted them by road to the LUMC, Leiden University Medical Center.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What else do we know?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not much. The patient's name, sex, nationality and condition haven't been released. The RIVM, the national public health institute, says they're being kept in strict isolation.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So here's the question everyone in Leiden is asking. Should I be worried?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The hospital and MSF both say no. They say there's no risk to other patients, visitors or the public, and visiting hours are unchanged. Health Minister Sophie Hermans says the LUMC is prepared to receive, screen and treat Ebola patients.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And that's not just reassurance. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of someone who's sick, not through the air. The LUMC has high-level isolation facilities and runs regular drills. And the Netherlands has done this once before. In 2014, a Nigerian UN peacekeeper from Liberia was treated at UMC Utrecht, and he was cured.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And how bad is it in Congo?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's grim. The outbreak was declared in May in Ituri province, and it's spread to North Kivu and several other provinces. It's the largest Ebola outbreak the country has ever recorded, with more than eight thousand confirmed cases and nearly four thousand deaths. MSF says the real toll is probably higher. And it's a rare strain, Bundibugyo, with no approved vaccine or treatment.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Three cases imported into Germany and France have all recovered. Everyone will be hoping the patient in Leiden is the fourth.

segments.title: Update: Heinen backs down on box 3

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, your savings, and a climbdown in The Hague.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Yesterday we told you that opposition parties, and even the coalition's own MPs, were rejecting the plan to cut the tax-free return in box 3, the wealth tax, to a thousand euros. On day two of the budget debate, Finance Minister Eelco Heinen gave way.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How far?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He called the criticism a 'clear signal' and said the cabinet is 'prepared to set a different threshold.' He also admitted he'd underestimated how many people would start paying tax on their savings. Estimates put it at around eight hundred and fifty thousand.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So what's the new number?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There isn't one yet, and he hasn't said how he'd pay for it. He says finding the money elsewhere is 'enormously complicated', because there are 'not many dials to turn'. He'll also take another look at next year's temporary cut to the tax-free allowance, but he made no promise to drop it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Remember, it's a minority cabinet. It needs opposition votes, and that gives the opposition real leverage. Heinen wants an answer by the Tax Plan debate in two weeks.

segments.title: EU halts aid to Sierra Leone amid Bolle Jos row

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, an aid freeze in West Africa, and the man often called the Low Countries' most wanted criminal.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Bolle Jos.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Bolle Jos, or 'Chubby Jos'. His real name is Jos Leijdekkers. The European Commission has stopped budget support to Sierra Leone with immediate effect. That's eighteen million euros this year for food programmes, education and infrastructure.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Quick who's who. Leijdekkers was sentenced in his absence to twenty-four years here, for cocaine trafficking and an attempted murder. In Belgium, his sentences add up to more than a hundred years. He's reported to have a child with the daughter of Sierra Leone's president. And the two countries have no extradition treaty.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Justice Minister David van Weel, from the centre-right VVD, has tied the freeze directly to him. He said Sierra Leone 'can solve this within twenty-four hours' by arresting and extraditing him. The Dutch want next year's payment stopped too.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So it really is about him?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This is where it gets messy. Officially, the Commission blames 'administrative errors', and NOS reports that Van Weel's comments irritated people there. Commissioner Magnus Brunner also gave 'technical' reasons, then added: 'We need Sierra Leone's cooperation. That is what this is about.'

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: There's a legal angle too. Budget support deals are binding contracts, and extradition isn't one of the conditions. So stopping the money over it wouldn't be allowed.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sierra Leone's government says the delay is procedural, and that EU officials told it this wasn't about any one person. It called the public pressure 'not conducive' to judicial cooperation.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Meanwhile, EU justice ministers have been discussing entry bans and asset freezes for criminals hiding outside Europe. This one isn't going quiet.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Back near Leiden now, where the coastal town of Katwijk has said yes to a huge pill factory.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The Eli Lilly one?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's the one. On Thursday evening, Katwijk's municipal council voted twenty-eight to four to give the American drugmaker a building permit. It's a three-billion-dollar plant near a lake called the Valkenburgse Meer.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: What'll it make?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Pills for diabetes and weight loss, including Lilly's GLP-1 tablet, orforglipron. There's a global race to build production capacity for these drugs. It should bring about five hundred jobs. And the CEO, David Ricks, says he picked Katwijk for the nearby airports and the Leiden Bio Science Park.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm guessing not everyone's thrilled.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: No. Hundreds of residents asked for an advisory referendum. The council turned that down the same evening, partly because it had to decide on the permit this week. Local parties KiesKatwijk and GemeenteBelangen were among those voting no. Residents worry about safety, the view, recreation at the lake, and, above all, water and energy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The water figure is striking. About eight hundred thousand litres of drinking water a day, roughly what all the households in the neighbouring village of Valkenburg use. And the energy side has a very Dutch twist: grid congestion. The power grid has no spare capacity for years, so at first the factory will make its own electricity with gas turbines.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Most of the council decided the economic benefits win out. Lilly still needs permits to start production and to discharge wastewater. When it announced the plan, it was aiming to start production in 2030.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Now, if you freelance here, or you hire freelancers, listen up.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The cabinet has published a draft Zelfstandigenwet, the Self-Employed Persons Act. It's meant to end years of uncertainty over who counts as a genuine freelancer, or zzp'er.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: For newcomers, a zzp'er is someone who's self-employed and has no staff. The tax authority has been cracking down on false self-employment. That's when people work like employees but are hired as freelancers to avoid payroll taxes. Clients risk back-tax claims, so a lot of them just stopped hiring freelancers altogether.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: So the minister, Thierry Aartsen, wants a clearer test. In practice, you'd be registered with the KvK, the Chamber of Commerce, and you'd have a VAT number and a business bank account. You send invoices. And you've had at least three different clients over two years, and you're actively looking for more.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And you get to decide where, when and how you work?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: In principle, yes, unless the job's tied to a place, like a building site. You'd also have to spend a minimum amount on things employees don't need, like disability insurance or a pension. That amount is still open. Aartsen says it mustn't be a 'wassen neus', literally a 'wax nose'. It means an empty gesture.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Great idiom. So how many people pass?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He reckons two-thirds to three-quarters of freelancers already do, or could fairly easily. If you pass, you no longer need to fear back-tax claims. But there's no transition period.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: ZZP Nederland supports the aims, but warns that clients mustn't shut freelancers out anyway, just to be safe. The union FNV Zelfstandigen has been sceptical. You can comment on the draft until the twenty-ninth of October, and it won't take effect before 2028.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: To the rivers now, which are so low that the boats meant to measure them can't get in.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Hang on, really?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Really. On the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and much of the Waal, the water is less than a hundred and twenty-five centimetres deep in places. Most of Rijkswaterstaat's survey boats sit deeper than that. Its three shallower boats are needed elsewhere too.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Rijkswaterstaat is the national roads and waterways agency. And those rivers are all branches of the Rhine, the freight route from Rotterdam into Germany. So why does measuring them matter?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Skippers use the shallowest measured point to work out how much cargo they can carry without running aground. Now they have to judge for themselves, or pay for commercial data. On the Upper IJssel, ships have been sailing one way at a time since late September, and some are taking detours of up to three hundred kilometres.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That has to show up in prices.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It does. The port of Rotterdam says about half as much cargo is moving between Rotterdam and the Rhine as a year ago. Shipping a tonne from Rotterdam to Cologne went from about seventeen euros in mid-June to eighty in early August. The inland shipping association calls it 'very worrying'.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Any relief in sight?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rijkswaterstaat says it needs rain, mostly upstream, outside the country. It says things won't get much worse, but they won't get much better either. And then there's a twist. An unusually warm sea could bring a very wet autumn, and high water after that.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: From too little water to too much. Peak Netherlands.

segments.title: Young Amsterdammers drink less, use more ketamine

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, a snapshot of what young Amsterdammers are drinking, taking and betting on.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's quite a menu.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's the annual Antenne Amsterdam monitor. It's commissioned by Jellinek, the city's best-known addiction care organisation, and published by the HvA, the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences. The headline is that young people are drinking less, but ketamine use in nightlife has risen sharply since 2024.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How do they know?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: They surveyed nearly twelve hundred MBO students, that's vocational college. They also interviewed nightlife insiders and youth workers, and looked at almost five thousand drug samples handed in for testing.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's a very Dutch data source. Here you can hand in drugs anonymously to find out what's actually in them. So, what is in them?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ketamine, MDMA and other powders cost about twenty-five to thirty euros a gram, and home delivery makes them easy to get. Demand for 3-MMC, a synthetic stimulant, has barely dipped since it was banned in July last year. And pills sold as 3-MMC often contain something else. Jellinek says 3-MMC carries a higher risk of dependence than ecstasy.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And laughing gas?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's nearly disappeared since the 2023 ban. Among the students, fifty-nine percent drank alcohol in the past year, and about half have ever vaped. Online gambling is becoming normal too. Almost one in five gambled online in the past year.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So is Gen Z swapping beer for cheaper drugs?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Jellinek's Jacqueline Krouwel says the study doesn't show that. Gen Z is simply drinking less overall.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if any of this hits close to home, Jellinek runs a helpline in Dutch and English, on weekdays from one to five in the afternoon.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, a surgical first from Nijmegen, and it left me asking why this took so long.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I'm intrigued.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Doctors at Radboudumc, Nijmegen's university hospital, have developed an operation to rebuild the clitoris after part of it is removed because of vulvar cancer. Until now, surgeons just closed the wound, and the clitoris disappeared under a layer of skin.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: How does the rebuild work?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: While they remove the tumour, surgeons free the clitoral nerve bundles and move them to form a new tip. Then they cover it with tissue from the inside of the cheek. It adds about fifteen minutes to the operation. In a first study of twenty-three women, ninety percent could have a clitoral orgasm again three to six months after surgery.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here's my favourite part. It all started because a patient simply asked whether reconstruction was possible. Oh, and a comparable operation for men with penile cancer has existed for almost forty years.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Forty years. Now all nine Dutch hospitals that treat vulvar cancer will learn the technique.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Credit to the patient who asked.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Sam, how do you get a seventeenth-century ship over a dike?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Carefully. Is this the Batavia?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It is. That's the full-size replica of a ship from the VOC, the Dutch East India Company, and it made its last voyage on Thursday. Tugboats towed it from the NDSM wharf in Amsterdam-Noord across the IJ, with crowds watching. Then it crossed the Markermeer to Museum Batavialand in Lelystad.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why is it the last voyage?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Wood rot. After about thirty years in the water, experts decided the hull couldn't stay afloat. So it's sitting in a steel frame on a pontoon. Today it gets driven off the pontoon, over the dike, and set down next to the museum. For good.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So it's a ship retiring to dry land. The original never got that chance. It left Texel in 1628 on its maiden voyage, went off course and was wrecked on reefs off Australia.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Work on the replica started in 1985, and Queen Beatrix christened it ten years later. The museum plans to restore it in stages, and to let visitors back on board when Batavialand reopens in 2028.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: A ship you can't sail, but you'll be able to climb aboard again. I'll take it.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And if you can't wait until 2028 for a day out, here's what's on in Amsterdam today. Camera Japan, the biggest Japanese film festival in the Benelux, is on at LAB111 in Oud-West. There's anime, arthouse, LGBTQ+ titles and classics, plus Japanese food, music and dance. Drop in any time from half past twelve until ten tonight.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The festival says times could still change, so check before you go. For jazz fans, the Bimhuis in Oost has Benjamin Herman's European Alto Festival at half past eight. It's a tribute to Piet Noordijk, with Spain's Irene Reig and Scotland's Rachael Cohen on alto sax. One night only.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And in the city centre, the Afrovibes festival is at De Brakke Grond from half past seven, with dance, theatre, music and spoken word by artists from Africa and the diaspora. It's there until Saturday, then it moves to Bijlmer Parktheater and Framer Framed.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Film, sax or spoken word. Take your pick.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: That's Dutch Daily Briefing for Friday. Thanks for listening, and have a lovely weekend.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: See you next time.
